929.text: The life of a geisha in pre-war Kyoto, lush with detail. Immersive and hard to put down.

1097.text: Schlosser pulls back the curtain on the American fast-food industry, from the feedlot to the counter. It'll change how you eat.

1103.text: A deep female friendship in 19th-century China, written in a secret women's language. Beautiful and heartbreaking.

1232.text: A boy in postwar Barcelona picks one book from the Cemetery of Forgotten Books, and it upends his life. Gothic, bookish, and totally transporting.

1618.text: A boy with a singular way of seeing the world sets out to solve the mystery of a dead dog and turns up much bigger ones. Tender and clever.

1848.text: Like Pachinko, Wild Swans is a beautifully written multigenerational saga spanning centuries and countries. Unlike Pachinko, it’s entirely true. Wild Swans charts the lives of three generations of Chinese women: a warlord’s concubine, a high Communist official, and the author herself, a Red Guard, then peasant, and finally student. It’s a memoir so compelling it reads like a novel.

1885.text: My favorite Austen, obviously. I reread it whenever I want to feel better about everything.

2156.text: Anne Elliot, older and wiser, gets a second chance at the love she was talked out of. Austen's most quietly romantic. That letter.

2187.text: The sweeping story of Cal, intersex, and three generations of a Greek American family. Eugenides makes the whole saga sing.

3008.text: Sara Crewe loses everything and holds onto her kindness anyway. I loved it fiercely as a kid, and it still gets me.

3636.text: The book that made a lot of us fall for dystopias. A boy discovers what his tidy, colorless world quietly traded away, and it stuck with me for years.

3686.text: Patchett's memoir of her fierce, complicated friendship with the writer Lucy Grealy. One of the great books about platonic love.

3711.text: Two tangled families in multicultural London across generations. Smith wrote this dazzler absurdly young.

3867.text: A lonely old man, a lost book, and a girl named after its heroine. Aching and beautifully made.

3985.text: Two cousins invent a comic-book superhero in the Golden Age while the war closes in on the family left behind in Europe. Chabon's sentences are a joy.

4214.text: A boy adrift on a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger, and a story about story itself. Strange and unforgettable.

4953.text: Eggers raising his little brother after both parents die, told with wild, self-aware energy. Funny and gutting.

5439.text: Lahiri's story collection about Indian and Indian American lives, longing and distance. Each one is quietly perfect.

5826.text: Bel Canto by Anne Patchett is, I think, her masterpiece. (And I’ve read all of her books!) The plot sounds like it’s ripped from an airport thriller: An opera singer is performing at a millionaire’s birthday party when terrorists take the entire mansion hostage. But what happens next is anything but predictable, and the prose is gorgeous. I read it every few years and recommend it to all of my friends.

5890.text: The Victorian mystery that basically invented the genre, and it still races along. Villains, secrets, and one unforgettable escape.

6185.text: Heathcliff and Cathy and a love that poisons everyone around it. Not romantic so much as feral — and I couldn't look away.

6334.text: Boarding-school kids whose purpose slowly, quietly reveals itself. Devastating in the calmest possible way.

7445.text: Like Educated, it’s a memoir of an incredibly gifted girl born into a dysfunctional family who, despite the odds, builds a new life. Both Educated and The Glass Castle take a clear-eyed but not dispassionate look at their parents and siblings — the beautiful and dark sides of their personalities, addictions, and failures.

9791.text: Bryson and his hopelessly unfit old friend attempt the Appalachian Trail. I laughed out loud more than once.

10210.text: One of my favorites, forever. Small, fierce Jane refuses to be anything but herself.

10441.text: A doctor secretly gives away his newborn daughter with Down syndrome and tells his wife she died. A decades-spanning novel about the weight of one lie.

13831.text: Alanna disguises herself as a boy to train as a knight. I devoured this whole series growing up.

14935.text: Austen on sisters — one all feeling, one all restraint. Not my top Austen, but still a delight.

14963.text: Seven old high school friends reunite at a Berkshires inn for a wedding, and a long-buried night from their past comes roaring back. Classic Shreve: warm, a little melancholy, quietly suspenseful.

15764.text: A story about a marriage that shouldn’t have happened. A gorgeous recreation of Baltimore from 1940s to present-day. I recommended it to Aliza, and she left me multiple voice notes about how much she loved it.

16527.text: A young Chilean woman stows away to Gold Rush California chasing her lover. Allende at her sweeping, romantic best.

29044.text: The Secret History by Donna Tartt is one of the books I’m jealous of other people for getting to read for the first time. In the opening sentence, you learn that a boy has been murdered, and the narrator, Richard, has helped murder him — the mystery, of course, is why. We go back in time, following Richard as he transfers to an elite New England college and becomes fascinated with a tight-knit, charismatic group of friends. The first time I read this book, I was completely carried away by the plot. The second (and third and fourth) times, I’ve been able to appreciate its exploration of beauty, morality, and the allure of belonging.

29579.text: Asimov's grand idea: a science that can predict the fall of a galactic empire, and one man's plan to soften the dark ages to come. Big, brainy, and surprisingly readable.

29580.text: The hunt for the hidden Second Foundation, with the Mule still looming. Asimov's ideas carry you right along.

29581.text: The Mule arrives and blows up Seldon's tidy plan for the galaxy. The most gripping stretch of the trilogy.

31661.text: A slim best-of from the master of the short story. If you've never read Munro, this is a lovely way in.

33917.text: Gogol Ganguli, saddled with an odd name, caught between his Bengali family and his American life. Quietly gorgeous.

37095.text: A big, warm family saga anchored by Penelope and a beloved painting. The kind of sprawling book you sink into for a week.

39963.text: A boy and his sister spend summers with their larger-than-life Grandma Dowdel in small-town Illinois. So funny.

41977.text: Binchy at her coziest, all friendship and first love and small-town Irish life in the '50s. Comfort reading that still has teeth.

43641.text: A Depression-era circus, a vet, and a forbidden romance. Immersive and a lot of fun.

45376.text: Three mismatched roommates at 1950s Harvard, and what loyalty and ambition do to them over the years. Quiet, precise, and very Henry James in the best way.

51108.text: Pei carries on from Women of the Silk, building a new life in Hong Kong through the war years. Quiet and moving.

51114.text: Girls in a Chinese silk factory who take vows never to marry and build a fierce sisterhood instead. Absorbing and tender.

62291.text: The best book in the series, full stop. If you've made it this far, brace yourself.

77156.text: Interwoven lives in a small Colorado town, including two old bachelor brothers who take in a pregnant teenager. Spare and deeply humane.

95961.text: Calvin Trillin's tiny, tender tribute to his late wife. You'll cry, and it's worth it.

113744.text: Lydia Davis can do more in two sentences than most writers manage in twenty pages. Tiny, strange, razor-sharp stories.

114447.text: A boy of mixed race in colonial India remakes himself over and over to survive. Ambitious and dazzling.

126849.text: An Irish-Catholic family in New York, seen through the kids being shuttled to their grandmother's apartment. McDermott makes the ordinary ache.

138556.text: Five girls at a New England prep school in the '60s, growing up as the Vietnam War and the women's movement crash into their sheltered world. It opens on their reunion, where we learn one of them didn't make it.

144977.text: Moehringer grew up fatherless, raised in part by the men at his uncle's bar. A warm, beautifully written memoir about the people who make you.

150739.text: Princess Cimorene is bored of being a proper princess, so she runs off to keep house for a dragon instead. I loved this as a kid — funny, fizzy, and quietly feminist.

167216.text: Strout's first novel, about a mother and teenage daughter in a Maine mill town and the affair that cracks them open. You can already see how good she is.

187020.text: A decent man running a diner in a dying Maine mill town, hemmed in by everyone's expectations. Russo's warmth and wit carry it.

201651.text: A First Lady goes on trial for murdering the philandering President. Buckley's satire is gleefully sharp.

234225.text: Politics, religion, ecology, and giant sandworms on a desert planet. A sci-fi cornerstone, and it earns it.

235773.text: A Chinese army doctor spends eighteen years waiting to divorce one woman and marry another. Quiet, patient, and quietly heartbreaking.

248704.text: A depressed teen checks himself into a psychiatric hospital. Honest, and more hopeful than you'd think.

256008.text: Two aging Texas Rangers drive cattle to Montana, and somehow it's 900 pages I never wanted to end. Funny, brutal, and completely alive.

306010.text: Fisher's sharp, hilarious semi-autobiographical novel about an actress in recovery and the Hollywood around her. She was so funny on the page.

355862.text: A Black novelist, sick of what publishing wants from him, writes a cynical parody that becomes a smash. Furious and very funny. The basis for American Fiction.

408837.text: King's debut, about a young American au pair for a family in France with its own quiet fault lines. You can already feel the writer she'd become.

430156.text: A woman who'll do anything for local TV fame, including talk a lovestruck teenager into murder. Maynard makes her chilling and weirdly funny.

448873.text: A quest fantasy narrated by a cocky young thief, and then that ending. I did not see it coming.

495395.text: A.J. Jacobs spends a year trying to follow every rule in the Bible literally. Funny and genuinely thoughtful.

500743.text: Heir Chronicles book two, following an untrained teenage wizard whose powers are spiraling out of control. Fun, fast contemporary fantasy.

701738.text: A grieving woman writes to Osama bin Laden after a terrorist attack takes her husband and son. Gutting.

897867.text: Children left mostly to themselves at a French hotel one hazy summer, right on the edge of growing up. Gorgeous and a little dangerous.

1379961.text: The imagined history of a real Hebrew manuscript, traced back across centuries. Loved the puzzle of it.

1432370.text: Liz Murray goes from homeless teenager to Harvard, and tells it without an ounce of self-pity. An genuinely inspiring survival memoir.

1627267.text: A girl's ex writes a hit breakup song about her and she becomes accidentally famous. Fun, loud YA.

1736739.text: Olive Kitteridge by Elizabeth Strout centers on Olive, a teacher living in coastal Maine — and one of my all-time favorite heroines. This book has an unusual structure: It’s a series of short stories revolving around Olive, letting us get to know her through different perspectives. She’s thorny yet compassionate, stubborn yet capable of growth. I feel like I understand her more deeply with each reading, and despite (or because of) her flaws, I see myself in her.

1796643.text: Aliza and I recently went to see Anne Lamott talk, and she lamented that no one reads Margaret Drabble anymore. I practically leapt out of my chair. “I do!!” I said. (Aliza leaned over and whispered: “overachiever.”) This book, a dark comedy about a marriage on the rocks, pulses with energy and life and feels shockingly contemporary.

1902241.text: A girl wakes from a long coma not quite herself, and slowly learns why. Quietly unsettling sci-fi.

2277185.text: A prim, down-on-her-luck governess stumbles into one glamorous, madcap day. Pure delight — I finished it grinning.

2429135.text: The thriller that got everyone hooked on Lisbeth Salander. Dark, twisty, and hard to put down.

2471029.text: The last of Elizabeth Jolley's Vera Wright trilogy, about a young woman who becomes maid to one sibling and mistress to another. Spare, tender, and quietly devastating — it swept the Australian book prizes for a reason.

2696181.text: A family sealed in an underground bunker for years — and the kid who starts to doubt why. Tense and creepy.

2964456.text: How Mandela used the 1995 Rugby World Cup to unite South Africa — the book behind Invictus. Inspiring.

2967752.text: I’m bringing my copy of The Elegance of the Hedgehog by Muriel Barbery, an unexpected and poignant novel about a 54-year-old apartment concierge in Paris who develops an unlikely friendship with a girl who lives in the building.

3525894.text: A Brown student spends a semester undercover at Jerry Falwell's Liberty University and comes away with real empathy. Curious and open-hearted, not smug — I loved that about it.

3591262.text: Twin brothers born of a nun in Ethiopia — medicine, betrayal, and family. Sprawling and rewarding.

5633771.text: A Princeton admissions officer whose careful life quietly unravels. More layered than the movie suggests.

6033525.text: The Donner Party told through one young bride's ordeal. Harrowing and hard to put down.

6081088.text: Krakauer's firsthand account of the 1996 Everest disaster he survived. I could not put it down and felt cold the whole time.

6101138.text: Thomas Cromwell's rise in Henry VIII's court, told from inside his head. Dense but brilliant — stick with it.

6240770.text: A.J. Jacobs runs a series of goofy life experiments — outsourcing his life, radical honesty — and reports back. Light and funny.

6366437.text: Jeannette Walls's 'true-life novel' about her tough, unstoppable grandmother out West. I loved this even more than I expected.

6401660.text: A Victorian con to swindle an heiress, and then a twist that flips the whole thing. Waters plots like a magician.

6432774.text: A journalist reports out his own addiction, interviewing everyone from his past. Ruthless and fascinating.

6456073.text: A hapless man starts over in bleak, beautiful Newfoundland. Proulx's prose is like nothing else, and I'd follow it anywhere.

6567412.text: Knapp's clear-eyed memoir of loving alcohol and then leaving it. Honest in a way that stays with you.

6573443.text: The stranger-than-fiction story of an ADM executive who turned FBI informant on a price-fixing scheme, then turned out to be his own kind of unreliable. Eichenwald makes corporate crime genuinely gripping.

6586497.text: Reichl reviewing New York restaurants in elaborate disguises so no one would recognize the critic. The food writing alone will make you starving.

7117958.text: A Jewish refugee tries to become the perfect Englishman by building a golf course. Charming and quietly moving.

7141642.text: David Mitchell drops you into a Dutch trading post off Japan around 1800 and doesn't let go. Dense but rewarding, with some unforgettable set pieces.

7331435.text: Interlinked stories about music, aging, and time — including that famous PowerPoint chapter. Dazzling.

7905092.text: Franzen doing what he does — a big, dysfunctional American family novel. Not everyone loves him but I got completely absorbed.

7937843.text: Narrated by a five-year-old who's only ever known one room. Claustrophobic, tender, and unforgettable.

8143909.text: A small Irish girl is sent to stay with relatives for a summer and finds unexpected tenderness. Perfect, and I mean perfect.

8172058.text: A prickly, socially clueless surgical intern gets courted by a fast-talking charmer. Lipman is so good at awkward, funny people.

8175835.text: The best sports memoir I've read. Agassi opens with 'I hate tennis' and it only gets more gripping from there.

8177569.text: Two neighboring marriages, decades apart, quietly entangle. Sue Miller understands people so well.

8218432.text: The Michael Eisner era at Disney in all its backstabbing glory. A doorstop, and I'd have read another hundred pages.

8550573.text: A linked short story collection following one woman from her preteens to adulthood. Its exploration of love, dating, and ambition is sharp and funny and wonderfully honest; I’ve read it multiple times and always notice something different.

8909152.text: A guy falls for a coworker by reading her flagged work emails — and can't figure out how to admit it. Rowell is charming and this one's a delight.

9118135.text: A researcher heads into the Amazon to track down a vanished colleague and a secretive drug trial. Patchett at her most adventurous.

9361589.text: A magical circus that only opens at night, with a slow-burn romance inside it. Pure enchantment.

9402168.text: Pfeffer's unsentimental take on how power actually works at work. Not always comfortable, but useful.

9684523.text: 17th-century Martha's Vineyard and the first Native American to graduate Harvard, seen through a minister's daughter. Vivid.

9938498.text: The American ambassador's family in Berlin as the Nazis rose to power. Reads like a thriller, and it's all true.

10054335.text: A whip-smart woman navigates 1930s New York society. Towles's writing is pure pleasure.

10062688.text: Febos's memoir of her years as a dominatrix while battling addiction. Unflinching and beautifully written.

10762469.text: After a Rapture-like event, it follows the ordinary people left behind. More about grief than the mystery.

10996342.text: College baseball, a fielding slump that spirals, and a handful of lives colliding at a small Wisconsin school. Warmer and more addictive than 'baseball novel' sounds.

11501957.text: A literary zombie novel set in a half-cleared Manhattan. Whitehead's prose is the real draw here. Bleak and brilliant.

11535564.text: Ruhlman goes deep on what it actually takes to cook at the highest level, from a brutal certification exam to Thomas Keller's kitchen. Will make you hungry and a little in awe.

11886692.text: A wickedly funny account of one woman's year-long engagement, and how a perfectly rational person slowly comes undone in the countdown to the wedding.

12168274.text: Christie building toward a single murder at a seaside house, with the crime saved for the end instead of the start. A clever twist on her own formula.

12415486.text: A food writer's marriage falls apart while she's pregnant, told with jokes and recipes. Bitter, hilarious, and over far too fast.

12965338.text: A sharp, funny teenage girl chafing against her strict Mennonite town. Toews makes you laugh and ache at once.

13158800.text: A lighthouse keeper and his wife keep a baby that washes ashore — and it wrecks everyone. Cried.

13325079.text: A squad of Iraq war soldiers paraded around a Dallas Cowboys game as heroes. Sharp, funny, and quietly furious about it.

13400892.text: Two best friends and the guy who comes between them. Funny and heartbreaking about how friendships bend and sometimes snap as you grow up.

13507212.text: Mantel's second Cromwell novel, following the fall of Anne Boleyn. Even better than Wolf Hall, I think.

13526165.text: Told through emails and documents as a genius, agoraphobic mom vanishes. So funny and clever.

13537029.text: Achilles and Patroclus, retold as a love story. You know how it ends and it still wrecks you.

13593564.text: Hanna Rosin's argument that women are pulling ahead across work and family. Provocative and full of data.

14781494.text: Simon Rich's very short, very funny stories about love. I laughed out loud more than once.

15507958.text: Yes, the quadriplegic-and-his-caregiver one. Cried, naturally.

15745753.text: Two misfit teenagers falling in love over mixtapes and comics in 1986. Cried, obviously.

15790842.text: Ursula Todd dies and is reborn again and again across the 20th century. Ingenious, and I couldn't stop.

15797715.text: Set during the Chechen wars, and somehow both devastating and full of grace. One of the best debuts I've read.

15798782.text: Four women take a road trip into their pasts. Berg is so good on the longings and regrets women carry, and this one goes down easy.

15815333.text: Friends who meet at an arts camp as teens, followed across decades of talent, envy, and money. Wolitzer nails how friendships shift over a lifetime.

15818333.text: Two sisters in Glasgow bury their parents and try to keep going alone. Dark, tender, and surprisingly funny.

15819028.text: A golem and a jinni, both new immigrants in 1899 New York, cross paths. Original and enchanting.

15990489.text: Maeve Binchy's last novel — a cast of guests converging on a seaside inn on the Irish coast. Cozy in the best way.

16066896.text: A washed-up writer bumps her head, gives a dazed interview, and accidentally becomes famous again. Wry and clever.

16068905.text: A shy college freshman who'd rather write fanfiction than face real life. So warm and true to being that age.

16077150.text: During the 1976 heatwave a father vanishes, and his grown kids reunite to figure out why. O'Farrell is wonderful on family.

16115612.text: Hosseini spanning generations and continents from one act of separation. He always wrecks me.

16126596.text: A brilliant, monstrous scientist recounts his discovery on a remote island. Dark and unsettling in the best way.

16131025.text: A Nantucket wedding and the late mother whose notebook is quietly running the whole thing. Prime Hilderbrand beach reading.

16158542.text: The University of Washington rowing team's improbable road to gold at the 1936 Berlin Olympics. I don't even care about rowing and I was riveted.

16181775.text: A socially oblivious genetics professor designs a questionnaire to find a wife. Charming and very funny.

17333223.text: A boy, a stolen painting, and years of fallout after a tragedy. Long, but Tartt's writing carries it.

17380041.text: Pride and Prejudice from the servants' side of the house. If you're an Austen fan, this is such a treat.

17383921.text: Jennifer Senior on why modern parenting is so joyful and so miserable at once. Well-reported and reassuring.

17465515.text: Book two of the Neapolitan novels, and the Lila-and-Elena friendship only gets more intense. If you loved the first, just keep going.

17884042.text: A famous photographer, broke and past her prime, decamps to a rented cottage and finds an unexpected late-life romance. Warm and wise.

17899948.text: A shy new bride at Manderley, haunted by the first Mrs. de Winter and the terrifying housekeeper who worshipped her. That opening line lives in my head.

17910118.text: A modern Jonah — a slick New York lawyer upended by visions he can't explain. Smart and unexpectedly big-hearted.

17934513.text: A woman holes up at her family's Sierra cabin to finish her dissertation and instead falls into a consuming affair. Huneven is so good on desire and self-sabotage.

18006389.text: A woman flying to Finland to leave her celebrated novelist husband, and the secret behind his success. Wolitzer is so sharp about marriage and ambition.

18039963.text: Amanda Lindhout's memoir of being kidnapped and held for more than a year in Somalia. Harrowing, and the resilience stays with you.

18054175.text: A grieving man writes letters to Richard Gere while trying to build a life. Odd, tender, and quietly funny.

18081809.text: A magic phone lets a woman call her husband in the past, back when things were good. Rowell for grownups, and lovely.

18104725.text: A funny, skeptical tour through the Nordic countries, poking at the myth that they've got it all figured out. Booth is a very entertaining guide.

18143977.text: A blind French girl and a German boy whose paths cross in occupied France. The writing is luminous, if occasionally too pretty. Beautiful and sad.

18209290.text: A ballet novel spanning defection, ambition, and a secret that reshapes a family. Shipstead writes dancers so well you feel the strain.

18240211.text: A boy eavesdrops on his mother's life and love affair as his parents' marriage collapses. Tender and a little heartbreaking.

18295861.text: A man who lives the same life over and over, keeping his memories each time — and someone is threatening the timeline. A clever, thoughtful spin on the time-loop idea.

18490557.text: Opens with the 1966 UT Austin tower shooting, then follows the lives it reshaped for decades. Quietly devastating.

18490619.text: Two best friends in New York hit the point where their lives start to diverge. Gould nails that specific late-twenties friendship ache.

18619684.text: A love story between a man who time-travels involuntarily and the woman who spends her life waiting for and loving him. Cried, naturally.

18630531.text: A young woman answers Salinger's fan mail at a stuffy old literary agency. A lovely coming-of-age for anyone who's dreamed of a life in books.

18641982.text: One family, one Mallorca vacation, every simmering tension along for the trip. The perfect beach read from Straub.

18668008.text: Two friends' real letters to each other as they flail through their twenties abroad. Funny and very relatable.

18693716.text: A broke single mom, her math-genius daughter, and an unlikely road trip. Sweet and easy to root for.

18867590.text: Rebecca Mead takes apart the American wedding industry and everything it sells us. Smart and a little rage-inducing, in the best way.

18892366.text: Lencioni's case that organizational health beats strategy. Simple, a little repetitive, but the core idea sticks.

18914754.text: Newly single sisters share a Manhattan apartment and slowly rebuild. Gentle, funny, and very good company.

19048697.text: A Jewish girl becomes quietly obsessed with a Vermont inn that won't take Jewish guests. Lipman turns prejudice into something wry and human without letting it off the hook.

19062459.text: Two families in the New York art world, and how love and loss ripple through both. Cerebral and devastating.

19100997.text: A woman comes home to her small New Hampshire town just as someone starts setting fires. Sue Miller is so good on family and low-grade dread.

19104786.text: A woman raised by a strange trio of adults tries to piece together her own past. Rachman is such a good storyteller.

19486412.text: Three moms, a school fundraiser, and a death we know is coming but not who. Moriarty's best — funny, twisty, and secretly about domestic violence. Loved it.

19792897.text: Two charismatic Tennessee brothers with more money than sense, half moonshine and half martini. It's a Southern Gatsby, and Majors clearly had a blast writing it.

20873740.text: Harari's whirlwind history of our species — how we went from one primate among many to running the planet. Big, provocative ideas, breezily told.

20910157.text: Amy Poehler's memoir, warm and funny and generous. Reads like she's talking right to you.

20928835.text: Nantucket, Christmas, one very messy family. Pure cozy Hilderbrand comfort reading.

21423525.text: A husband tries to save his marriage on a family tour of Europe. Funny and sad in that very Nicholls way.

22015256.text: A comic novel about two kids scheming to find their newly-divorced mother a husband. Wickedly funny.

22085568.text: The clearest thing I've read on why people from different cultures clash at work. Genuinely useful.

22318513.text: A sweeping novel about a genius mathematician and the wreckage he leaves behind. Ambitious and completely absorbing.

22367526.text: A Baton Rouge coming-of-age wrapped around the crime that happened to the girl next door. Nostalgic and tense at once.

22749994.text: Hornby on a 1960s British sitcom star and the men who write her show. Warm and full of affection for comedy.

22822858.text: A brutal, beautiful, devastating novel about four friends and the trauma one of them carries. Be warned it's a lot — I sobbed. Not for everyone but I couldn't shake it.

22929602.text: A spare, intense novel about an American teacher's obsession with a young hustler in Bulgaria. Greenwell writes desire and shame beautifully.

23156040.text: Book three, and the friendship gets thornier and more real. I tore through all four.

23398625.text: Told through linked stories about food and the people orbiting one gifted chef. Warmer and cleverer than I expected.

23444482.text: A conquered girl becomes an accountant for the empire that destroyed her home, planning to burn it down from inside. A ruthless, brainy fantasy — the ending wrecked me.

23492673.text: An anthropologist 'studies' the ultra-wealthy mothers of the Upper East Side like a lost tribe. Funny and a little unbelievable — a guilty pleasure.

23602552.text: A married couple retreats to the countryside, and a new neighbor cracks everything open. Black writes quiet marital tension beautifully.

24612118.text: A marriage told first from his side, then hers — and hers changes everything. Groff's writing is dazzling; the second half is the whole game.

24911006.text: 4.5 I finished Missoula a couple of days ago, and I can't stop thinking about it. It's a searing account of the "rape crisis" that occured at the University of Montana over four years. (Krakauer cites national campus sexual assault statistics as evidence this wasn't a crisis at all; it's actually on par with average.) It's non-fiction, but I couldn't put it down. Krakauer does an excellent job dis

25242224.text: The finale of the Neapolitan quartet — a stunning, gutting end to Lenù and Lila.

25667449.text: Olivia Laing weaves her own loneliness in New York through the lives of artists who were lonely too. Melancholy and gorgeous.

25781157.text: Four grown siblings, one dwindling inheritance, and endless family dysfunction. Funny and sharp — I tore through it.

25814219.text: A quirky, tightknit family running a struggling record store in '90s New York. Sweet and a little heartbreaking, with a lot of love packed in.

25852870.text: A modern-day Pride and Prejudice set in Cincinnati, and enormous fun. No one does banter and human foibles better than Sittenfeld.

25899336.text: A young neurosurgeon writes about his own dying as terminal cancer takes hold. Unbearably moving and somehow not depressing. Cried, of course.

26114644.text: A wealthy, comically eccentric New England family narrated by a reclusive daughter with a secret online life. If you like Anne Tyler's quirky families, this scratches the same itch.

26155161.text: A hospitalized woman and her difficult mother, in Strout's spare, aching prose. Quiet and powerful.

26192646.text: A young woman falls into the world of an upscale New York restaurant — the wine, the drugs, the exhaustion. Danler makes you taste all of it.

26256492.text: Stories set in the stark, gorgeous country around Wyoming's Wind River Reservation, full of cowboys, cops, and vets, where small events tip the ordinary into something like the miraculous. Everett in a quieter register.

26811738.text: A clear, useful primer on how platform businesses actually work. Handy if you spend time thinking about tech and network effects.

26890725.text: A sharp, honest look at a lifelong female friendship that's grown lopsided. Alam is so good on the small resentments.

33778610.text: A Nigerian marriage strained to breaking by infertility and family pressure. Gutting.

48912823.text: A woman drowning in debt and precarity in New York, even with the 'right' life on paper. Spare and quietly furious.

48914611.text: A cellist's carefully planned summer in Connecticut falls apart when her breakup and her two grown kids all land on her doorstep at once. Funny, warm, and full of family chaos.

48990389.text: A woman traverses parallel universes — but can only visit worlds where her other self is dead. Fresh, propulsive sci-fi.

48999153.text: A clear, non-judgmental handbook on spotting and stopping the little slights that push people out at work. Genuinely useful if you care about making everyone feel like they belong.

49100158.text: Luster is the most gripping book I've read in a long time. Like other reviewers, I picked it up for a bit of casual reading—and found myself, two hours later, still in the same place, gorging myself on Raven Leilani's prose. I've read other unputdownable books before. However, these are usually suspense/thrillers, like Gone Girl. The plot isn't "the thing" in Luster. The plot is a vehicle for Leil

49201438.text: A broke actress scores an invite onto a billionaire's Mediterranean yacht, and things go sinister fast. A fun, twisty summer thriller — perfect beach read.

49447605.text: A former child star confronts the director who abused her. Timely and sharply observed.

49856101.text: The story behind the death of Shakespeare's son, centered on his wife. Luminous. I cried.

49914109.text: The memoir of America's youngest sommelier — the grind, the sexism, the wine. Fast and juicy.

49982087.text: A sweeping Australian family saga and a forbidden love that spans decades. Big, old-fashioned, and totally absorbing.

50027315.text: A slim, aching novel about the love between two men and the woman who loved them both. It wrecked me.

50042494.text: Its narrator, 32-year-old Nina Dean, is more established than Rooney’s heroines but just as relatable, quick-witted, and candid. Nina’s life is complete in all ways but one — her career as a food writer is thriving, she lives in a beautiful London apartment, and her platonic relationships are wonderful. She doesn’t, however, have a partner. Then she meets the perfect guy, and we’re off to the races. Until he ghosts her…

50045075.text: A teen boy and his volleyball-star neighbor in a violent, tender suburban friendship. Rufi Thorpe is fearless.

50065605.text: A remote Norwegian island after a storm kills the men, then the witch hunts begin. Atmospheric and tense.

50130587.text: The memoir behind a beloved anonymous Twitter persona, and how inventing her helped a real, lonely woman. Unexpectedly moving.

50158413.text: Wizenberg's memoir about falling for a woman in her forties and rethinking everything she assumed about herself. Honest and searching.

50196744.text: Chanel Miller reclaims her story from the Brock Turner case. Devastating, furious, and beautifully written — everyone should read it.

50209521.text: Aron's memoir of loving an addict and her own pull toward codependency. Fierce and clear-eyed.

50240841.text: Three people navigate an unexpected pregnancy and what family even means. Sharp, messy, and completely original.

50408097.text: An Irish woman in Hong Kong, torn between a banker and a lawyer. Wry, cool, and very smart.

50536943.text: The book I want to hand every friend I'm scared of drifting from. Sow and Friedman take a close friendship seriously enough to examine how it almost broke.

50888243.text: A Brooklyn housing project in 1969, after an old deacon shoots a drug dealer in broad daylight. Sprawling, funny, and full of life.

51003468.text: I was never a big romance reader... until the pandemic. When the world feels like it's burning down around you, it turns out a light-hearted romp is exactly what you need. And The Roommate is no different. If you enjoyed The List, , Evvie Drake Starts Over, and/or any of Elinor Lipman's books, you'll like The Roommate. Pros: It was refreshing to get another take on the adult entertainment industry

51046755.text: Two sisters in Philadelphia — one a cop, one lost to addiction — set against the opioid crisis. Part mystery, part family story, all propulsive.

51117957.text: Susan Fowler's blog post about Uber's toxic culture blew the company open. Her memoir is even more infuriating and impressive than you'd expect.

51226935.text: The teenage daughter of a French politician's mistress decides to blow up the secret. Elegant and quietly explosive.

51340472.text: A young woman survives her brutal first years at a cutthroat BigLaw firm. Juicy and propulsive.

51375432.text: Konnikova learns high-stakes poker to understand luck and self-control, and turns it into the best kind of psychology book. Fascinating.

51457980.text: A college assault story told through shifting genres and unreliable voices. Unsettling and inventive.

51608211.text: A 'Same Time Next Year' setup: two people meet one weekend a year for decades. Hilderbrand at her most emotional. I cried.

51837291.text: A story collection anchored by a knockout title novella about history and race. Danielle Evans is so sharp.

51907346.text: A grandmother witnesses a sudden death and starts telling her family the truths she's held back. Straub at her warm, generous best.

52085140.text: 1883 London, delivered as the wit-soaked diary of one very sharp young woman navigating eccentric relatives and odd neighbors. If you love Austen or Wodehouse, this is pure comfort reading.

52141950.text: Spring training in Arizona, told through a whole cast — a star player unraveling, an aging coach, an agent in decline. Even if you don't love baseball, the characters carry it.

52194898.text: The inside story of Instagram — the founders, the sale, the culture shift. Gossipy and genuinely illuminating.

52195151.text: Twin sisters split — one passes as white, one doesn't — and their lives diverge for decades. Gorgeous and gripping.

52237660.text: A forty-six-year-old woman keeps spotting her twenty-two-year-old self around New York. A strange, smart novel about memory, regret, and the roads you didn't take.

52358404.text: A broke musician gets hired to play for a group of glossy mommy influencers, and things curdle. A juicy, satirical page-turner.

52476830.text: A mother certain something is wrong with her daughter, and no one believes her. A chilling, propulsive read about motherhood's dark side.

52545816.text: Light on celebrity gossip, but the best description of chronic illness I've ever read. While Dunham isn't a reliable narrator, she's an incredible one.

52593527.text: A genuinely practical guide to building and running distributed teams — hiring, onboarding, communication, culture across time zones. The recommendations are backed by real case studies and data, not just vibes.

52597312.text: David Mitchell follows a made-up London band through the psychedelic '60s. Fun and full of heart, with his usual sneaky connections to his other books.

52696974.text: A young opera singer in London gets entangled with a much older man. Sharp about art, money, and self-erasure.

52702097.text: A strange, beautiful novel about a man who lives alone in a labyrinthine house filled with statues and tidal halls… and slowly comes to realize he doesn’t know who he is or how he got there. It’s unlike anything else, and somehow both deeply weird and deeply moving.

52759167.text: A memoir about an abusive relationship — except Machado wrote it like a literary Choose Your Own Adventure. Each chapter turns the same story over in the light from a different angle. It’s formally unlike anything else on this list, and it moves fast.

52873094.text: A glamorous 1950s socialite investigates a creepy house in the Mexican countryside. Gorgeous and genuinely eerie.

52894214.text: Birbiglia on becoming a dad when he really wasn't sure he wanted to be. Funny and honest in the way only he can pull off.

52918279.text: A young Chinese American woman, part thief, claws toward the life she wants. Dark, addictive, morally slippery.

53011908.text: Ronan Farrow's account of chasing the Weinstein story past every attempt to kill it. Reads like a spy thriller.

53341634.text: Fifty-one-year-old twins who've never left home suddenly lose their mother, and everything they relied on starts to unravel into hardship and buried family secrets. Won the Costa. Bleak and beautiful.

53507736.text: A long marriage, a sudden death, and a secret the widow uncovers. Tender and painfully true.

53677457.text: We Keep the Dead Close: A Murder at Harvard and a Half Century of Silence by Becky Cooper is a memoir spanning continents and centuries, from Cooper’s memories of going to Harvard in 2009 to a dig in Tepe Yahya, Iran, in 1968. Although I’m not typically a true crime lover, the excellent writing and Cooper’s eventual connection between the murder and the Me Too movement kept me captivated.

53746844.text: A woman burned by men invents a 'perfect' fake self to date as. Angry and funny and more moving than I expected.

53867504.text: A vacation rental, a mysterious blackout, and two families stuck together. Dread you can't shake.

53923958.text: A woman working a chip shop in a small Northern Irish town, told in her singular voice. Funny, dark, and completely alive.

54310999.text: A grieving furniture designer at a relentlessly cheerful company falls for the wrong person. Deadpan and satisfying.

54383963.text: A marriage on the rocks, two spies with secrets, and a daughter who goes missing in Barcelona. A fast, twisty thriller for when you want to tear through something in a weekend.

54385373.text: A woman with an eating disorder falls for a zaftig Orthodox Jewish woman at a frozen-yogurt shop. Broder is filthy, funny, and raw.

54640667.text: Twelve interlinked Black British women across generations, in Evaristo's rushing, near-verse style. Ambitious and wonderful.

54746196.text: Set at a Deaf boarding school, with real ASL and Deaf culture woven in. Immersive and eye-opening. I learned a ton.

54846475.text: A gang of retirees in a posh care home solve murders. Cozy, clever, and genuinely funny.

55071877.text: Two estranged Korean-American sisters collide in New York when one gets sick. Choi is funny and unsparing about family.

55360284.text: Stanley Tucci on a life measured in meals. Charming, generous, and yes, it will make you hungry.

55372861.text: A pandemic that kills only men reshapes the world. Eerily prescient and hard to put down.

55434914.text: A biracial young woman nannies for a wealthy Manhattan family, never quite belonging anywhere. Quiet and sharp on class and not fitting in.

55468002.text: A rich, beautiful woman decides to sleep through an entire year with the help of a terrible psychiatrist. Bleak, hilarious, iconic.

55556143.text: A domestic thriller with a great hook — what if husbands did their fair share, and what it took to get there. Sharp about the mental load, and fun.

55577549.text: Zauner — the musician behind Japanese Breakfast — wrote this memoir after losing her Korean mother to cancer. It’s about grief, yes, but mostly it’s about food as love language, and what happens when the person who fed you is gone. Multiple friends have finished it in a single sitting, then called their mothers. You will too.

55590431.text: A young woman assisting a famous anonymous author gets pulled into something sinister. A clever, twisty ride.

55758388.text: A Nantucket novelist dies and watches her family's summer unfold from above. Classic Hilderbrand comfort with a twist.

55886036.text: A man saves a stranger from drowning and then can't stop watching what happens to him. A tight, twisty literary thriller. Gulped it.

55939506.text: Horror-movie 'final girls' meet in group therapy decades later, then get hunted again. So clever and so fun.

55985254.text: A sheltered teen nannies for a family hiding a rock star in rehab, 1970s Baltimore. Warm and joyful.

56007910.text: A bedridden novelist starts getting calls from a woman who doesn't exist. A slippery little thriller.

56050608.text: A woman's marriage and mind unravel, and it's somehow hilarious and devastating at once. I adored this.

56124750.text: Interlinked stories about money, love, and luck rippling between strangers. Silber makes it look effortless.

56247202.text: Franzen at his most humane — a Midwestern pastor's family quietly coming apart in the early '70s. Dense and totally absorbing.

56343711.text: The definitive account of the Sacklers and the fortune they built on OxyContin. Infuriating and impossible to put down.

56378432.text: A marriage and a friendship crack open over a long-buried secret. Sweeney is great on midlife and disappointment.

56519331.text: A daring female aviator and the actress playing her decades later. Sweeping and immersive — I loved every page.

56665711.text: Two broke young women charm their way through a New York summer. Frothy, sharp, and so much fun.

56665713.text: Rooney doing what Rooney does — smart people, long emails, and a lot of feelings. I'm always in.

56665714.text: An obsessive, corrosive love affair in Dublin, told from inside the wreckage. Raw and uncomfortably honest.

56691215.text: A childfree woman navigates friendships and a life that looks different from everyone else's. Warm and validating.

56748012.text: A Vietnamese family's hard first years in Queens, told by the daughter who translated their whole world. Beautiful and clear-eyed.

56761975.text: A real 17th-century witch trial, narrated by the cranky woman on trial. Funny and unexpectedly warm.

56787087.text: Jia Tolentino's essays on the internet, scams, and being alive right now. Whip-smart — she notices things you didn't have words for.

56894210.text: Enormous and ambitious — generations of one Black American family threaded through centuries of history. Worth the commitment.

57012630.text: Two friends named Emily, 90s New York, and the way close friendships shift over decades. Kois nails the ache of growing up and apart.

57108122.text: Art school and the New York art world, told through students and a fading painter. Angress is sharp about ambition and money.

57123268.text: A stay-at-home mom becomes increasingly convinced she's turning into a dog. Feral, funny, and weirdly cathartic.

57182435.text: 1950s England, a lonely journalist, and a woman claiming a virgin birth. Quiet, tender, and it wrecked me.

57196244.text: A queer coming-of-age where a young photographer accidentally lands in the modeling world. Tender writing about bodies, movement, and figuring out who you are.

57329182.text: A Baltimore family traced across decades and all the small ways they drift apart and find each other again. Quintessential Anne Tyler.

57356972.text: A court interpreter at The Hague, unmoored in a foreign city. Cool, precise, and quietly unsettling.

57378707.text: Two writers who had one scorching teenage week reconnect twenty years later. Sexy, smart, and full of heart.

57452610.text: An aging professor becomes obsessed with a younger male colleague while her husband faces accusations. Wickedly smart and uncomfortable.

57602357.text: Colwin writing about happy people in love, which sounds boring and is somehow the opposite. Warm, witty, and completely charming.

57640897.text: Matrix is a mostly fictional novel about a real person: Marie de France, an orphaned poet and member of the twelfth century royal court who is banished to a nunnery. She’s an incredible protagonist: clever, ambitious, and fiercely independent. Anyone who fell in love with Circe’s dynamism will be captivated by Matrix.

57675954.text: A Tokyo wife, restless in her marriage, meets someone new. Wry and aching in equal measure.

57696105.text: A former teen-show cast reunites years after everything imploded. Fun, dishy, and sharper about fame than you'd expect.

57768107.text: A sharp Australian campus novel about consent, betrayal, and who gets to tell the story. Reid is scary smart.

58061810.text: One momentous day at a Cape Cod summer house, with a lifetime of choices behind it. I inhaled this.

58184393.text: This debut novel, a letter from a son to a mother who cannot read, is more than anything a work of poetry, one so rich and moving it clearly draws on lived experience. I’m not a big re-reader, but I’d like to go back to both of these.

58256450.text: A mother has one bad day and gets sent to a government institution to prove she deserves her child. Chilling, and a little too plausible.

58262351.text: Tender, funny, and a little heartbreaking — a young gay man in Seoul, his mother, and the men he loves. I tore through it.

58268352.text: A quartet of nuns gets relocated to run a halfway house in Rhode Island. Odd, funny, and unexpectedly moving.

58283993.text: A grandmother takes in her granddaughter when her own daughter's addiction makes things impossible. Quietly devastating and so wise about the limits of love. Cried, naturally.

58395053.text: A young writer works as a groundskeeper in Kentucky and falls for someone out of his class. Cole is thoughtful about place and belonging.

58416952.text: A Roman-inspired fantasy where power is literally something people surrender. Twisty, propulsive, and I did not see the ending coming.

58448487.text: Ballet, New York, and a young man's fractured family and two estranged fathers. Howrey writes about art and love beautifully.

58460887.text: A day in the life of a Hollywood producer's fixer, with a scandal about to blow. Fun, propulsive, and smart about power.

58533799.text: Linked stories tracing two Taiwanese American friends across years and coasts. Quietly a love story about friendship.

58556596.text: A brilliant 1960s chemist gets pushed out of science and becomes an unlikely TV cooking-show star. Charming and a little righteous.

58596754.text: A young woman comes home to care for her dying father, narrated by the town's cemetery dead. Odd, tender, and full of heart.

58601245.text: Time travel, a moon colony, and a quiet meditation on pandemics and art. Mandel is doing something special. Loved it.

58706017.text: A heartbroken man walks from New York to Arizona and slowly rejoins the world. Gentle and surprisingly moving.

58794688.text: Two college friends on a canoe trip in the far north race a wildfire — and stumble into something worse. Tense and gorgeous.

58804393.text: Philpott's essays on anxiety, aging parents, and loving people in a fragile world. Warm and quietly wise.

58812692.text: A remote town where mothers occasionally just vanish, and no one questions it. Schaitkin builds eerie, dreamlike unease. I couldn't stop.

58812701.text: A teenage girl's sister vanishes, and years later the boyfriend reappears. Espach is funny and devastating by turn.

58864196.text: The queen bee of a Christian Alabama school disappears, leaving clues. A smart, swoony McQuiston YA. Delightful.

58916147.text: Two friends build video games and a lifelong bond across thirty years. It's about creative partnership and love that isn't romance. So good.

58941191.text: A wild insider account of how the ultra-rich really operate in China — and how fast it can all turn on you.

58949321.text: A newly-widowed woman decamps to the French Riviera with her sister and their old wounds. Glamorous and prickly in a good way.

59016923.text: A coal merchant in small-town Ireland has to decide whether to look away. Tiny book, enormous moral weight. Cried, naturally.

59055336.text: A broke rare-book dealer falls in with occult sex magic and a very charming partner in crime. Sexy and pulpy in the best way.

59109017.text: A tender, funny novel about a long female friendship and a woman quietly falling apart. Stibbe is so warm.

59142475.text: A May-December marriage in New York unravels amid art, money, and addiction. Mellors writes glossy people with real feeling.

59227941.text: Classic beachy Hilderbrand — a rundown Nantucket hotel, a big cast, and a little bit of ghost. Exactly the summer read it promises to be.

59363539.text: A big Irish-American family and their Chicago restaurant in the weird aftermath of 2016. Funny and full of people you recognize.

59422043.text: Two women run a counterfeit-handbag scheme, told as a very unreliable confession. Clever, twisty, and a blast.

59425313.text: Grady Hendrix does grief through a haunted-house horror full of demonic puppets. Genuinely scary and secretly about family.

59438099.text: A woman turns 40, then wakes up at 16 with her young, healthy father downstairs. A time-travel novel that's really about loving your parents. I teared up.

59557275.text: Warm, funny food essays that read like your smartest friend telling kitchen stories. Made me want to cook and to write better about cooking.

59563482.text: Everything you'd want to know about Anna Wintour and how she became Anna Wintour. Odell makes the Vogue machine fascinating.

59603040.text: A wealthy old man's much-younger girlfriend versus his scheming adult daughter. A nasty, twisty little pleasure.

59722217.text: Follows a boy named Sam growing up over many years, in small tender increments. Allegra Goodman does ordinary life beautifully.

59767161.text: Three sisters orbiting a mother whose warmth keeps tipping into darkness. A debut about class, inheritance, and everything daughters carry. Beautifully done.

59771967.text: Auletta's exhaustive account of Weinstein and the machine that protected him for decades. Damning and thorough.

59788021.text: A young woman drifts into a relationship with a man twenty years older in a sleepy Australian beach town. A debut about desire and memory that just aches.

59808037.text: Cara Romero is 56, recently unemployed, and reporting to a government job program in 1980s New York. The whole novel is just her talking — to her caseworker, across a desk, week after week. It’s funny and sad and textured. Now that I think about it, it’d be a great follow-up read to The Correspondent.

59912890.text: A young writer falls into an intense affair with an older choreographer. Sharp about power, desire, and who you become for someone.

60065460.text: A young woman's affair with an older woman, and how it shapes her years later. Quiet, moody, and precise.

60194162.text: Kingsolver reworks David Copperfield into Appalachia and the opioid crisis, and it's devastating. That kid's voice will wreck you.

60197744.text: Two poor girls in rural France, one story they can't stop telling. Li writes friendship as something closer to possession.

60277011.text: I love reality TV, especially Survivor, so this debut about a survival reality show gone wrong was right up my alley. Tense and more thoughtful than I expected.

60372100.text: A gothic horror where a poor girl takes a job at a sinister estate feeding on 'blood maids.' Dark and atmospheric.

60394519.text: Renaissance Italy and the teenage duchess Lucrezia de' Medici, married off and afraid. O'Farrell's writing is stunning.

60396325.text: Qureshi's memoir of falling in love on her own terms as a British Pakistani woman. Gentle and lovely.

60417006.text: An elderly woman in a care facility starts to doubt what's real. Reid does dread better than almost anyone. Unsettling.

60429621.text: Hsu's memoir about a college friendship cut short by violence. Tender and precise about who we are at twenty. Deserved the Pulitzer.

60466391.text: A murdered woman is brought back as a clone and starts investigating her own death. A propulsive, weird little thriller with real ideas.

60582779.text: Essays circling a called-off wedding, marriage, and how we love. The title essay alone is worth it.

60607196.text: A church committee searching for a new minister, with recipes. Huneven makes small-group politics weirdly gripping and funny. Loved it.

60699135.text: A woman falls hard for a man in recovery, knowing exactly how it might end. Halperin makes the ache feel completely real.

60755035.text: Two bored teens make one weird poster and accidentally spark a town-wide panic. Wilson is funny and humane as always.

60867170.text: The harrowing story of a cruise ship stranded as COVID hit. Reads like a thriller, and it actually happened.

61055826.text: A lawyer under house arrest strikes up a romance with a neighbor in the same boat, and starts cooking. Breezy and charming, classic Lipman.

61077851.text: Two women in their eighties, lifelong friends, and a stretch of Maine coast they're fighting over. Rich and slow in the best way.

61090779.text: Franco makes the science of adult friendship feel urgent and doable. I underlined half of it and immediately texted three people.

61118631.text: An athlete marries into royalty and finds herself gilded and trapped. Bourland makes the cage claustrophobic and beautiful.

61133361.text: Hell as a soul-crushing bureaucracy, plus a family secret. A dark, clever premise pulled off with real wit.

61189184.text: Northern Ireland during the Troubles, a young teacher and an older married man. Kennedy writes tension you can feel in your chest. Excellent.

61190770.text: Prisoners fight to the death on live TV for a shot at freedom. A furious, unforgettable indictment of American incarceration.

61192679.text: A single mom slowly comes undone and lands in a state hospital, and her three kids are left to grow up in the wreckage. Quiet, devastating, told with so much tenderness.

61310894.text: A chaotic, big-hearted comedy set around a New York brownstone. Poeppel is reliably delightful.

61313251.text: Two kids raised in a fundamentalist church fall for each other and spend fifteen years unable to let go. An unconventional, slow-burn love story I couldn't put down.

61322427.text: A decades-long friendship between two women trying to make it in New York. It captures how a friendship can be its own great love story, and its own heartbreak.

61660241.text: An SNL-style writer falls for the pop star hosting the show and refuses to believe it could work. Smart, swoony, very fun.

61854923.text: A shipwreck, a mutiny, and rival survivors telling wildly different stories. Grann makes nonfiction read like a thriller.

61986846.text: A pitch-black comedy about the death of a celebrity chef and the frantic, self-serving scramble around it. Wickedly fun.

62039166.text: An Irish family unravels one member at a time, each section funnier and sadder than the last, building to an ending I'm still not over. Long but I inhaled it.

62067054.text: A beautiful twenty-something is staying with her older lover on Long Island. She flirts with someone else in front of him, and he kicks her out. Most people would go home… but Alex stays. Typically, after a few months, a book’s plot becomes hazy — I read this one three years ago and could write the Wikipedia plot summary.

62084507.text: A devastating and gorgeous WWI story about two teenage boys who fall in love in the trenches. It will wreck you. If you finished Shuggie Bain, Demon Copperhead, and/or The Heart’s Invisible Furies, and wanted more, this one’s for you.

62601701.text: A tabloid reporter circles an Irish family in London after a child dies, and Nolan slowly peels back what really happened. Bleak and beautifully written.

62606735.text: An autistic woman's carefully ordered life gets upended when a magnetic couple moves in next door and sets their sights on her teenage daughter. Longlisted for the Booker, and the narrator's voice is unforgettable.

62646531.text: Helen Ellis is so funny. These are warm, wickedly funny little essays about staying happily married.

62886088.text: A charming Australian rom-com about roommates and a very ill-advised deal. Sweet and quick.

62902483.text: The Redstone media empire, the palace intrigue, the money and family rot. Stewart makes corporate drama read like a soap opera.

63222079.text: One kid falls from a window and four suburban families crack open. Audrain knows exactly how to keep you turning pages.

63247365.text: Two writers with a tragic shared history end up in the same TV writers' room, forced to reckon with each other. A romance with real emotional weight under the banter.

63256933.text: An older woman tells her daughters about the summer she spent performing alongside — and falling in love with — a now-famous actor. My friend Anna said her husband adored this book just as much as she did — impressive, considering he typically reads business non-fiction.

63853404.text: A guerrilla-gardening collective and a sinister billionaire collide in New Zealand. A thriller with brains. I tore through it.

63892606.text: Heiny's stories are wry, warm, and full of people making a mess of their lives. She's just so easy to love.

65648032.text: A Black woman and her conservative white coworker fall for each other at Goldman Sachs. Uncomfortable, provocative, and genuinely made me argue with it.

73971348.text: Two broke friends in Cork get tangled up in a married professor's life. Warm, chaotic, and I loved every page.

74831628.text: Pittard writes about her husband's affair with her best friend, and somehow it's funny and raw at once. The 'kind of' in the subtitle earns itself.

74891998.text: A man is diagnosed with a condition that's slowly turning him into a great white shark, and his wife has to let him go. Weird premise, real heartbreak.

74896591.text: One affair unravels a tight-knit Jewish family in Boston, one member at a time. Smart and readable.

85323183.text: A quietly damning novel that follows one woman's career into the oil industry. Kiesling makes ambition and complicity feel intimate.

101404407.text: American wives in early-'60s Saigon and the good intentions that curdle. McDermott looking hard at who gets to feel virtuous.

122892583.text: A creepy, slow-tightening novel narrated by a girl obsessed with her charismatic teacher. Chidgey is so controlled it's unnerving.

125622460.text: A TV writer (Friends, Breaking Bad) on why she walked away from Hollywood. Blunt, funny, and refreshingly unsentimental about the dream job.

127282939.text: A girl who's pretty sure she's an alien faxes her observations about Earth back home. Weird, funny, and it completely won me over.

127463471.text: An RA, a visiting writer, and a lot of money changing hands in an Arkansas dorm. Kiley Reid is so sharp about class and wanting things.

133287167.text: Sloane Crosley on losing her closest friend to suicide, braided with a burglary. Funny and raw at once.

135984288.text: The unauthorized story of Ray Dalio and the strange, cultish culture he built at Bridgewater. A very juicy corporate-implosion read.

138505710.text: Naomi Klein keeps getting mistaken for Naomi Wolf and follows that thread down into conspiracy culture and our strange mirror world. Fascinating.

155685405.text: Jamison on new motherhood and the end of her marriage, all in that precise, aching prose. She never lets herself off the hook.

177058836.text: A town bordered by the same valley twenty years in the past and twenty years ahead, and a girl who has to guard the line. Haunting premise, beautifully done.

177328214.text: A woman checks into a grand hotel at her lowest and gets pulled into a stranger's over-the-top wedding. Warmer and funnier than that sounds.

195372149.text: Every time a husband goes up to the attic, a new one comes down, with a whole new life attached. A wildly clever premise that's secretly about choice.

195391626.text: A journalist digs into why adult friendships are so hard to keep, and offers actual scripts and strategies for holding onto the people who matter. Practical and validating.

195853578.text: Three college friends from the '90s reunite for their delayed 25th reunion in the summer of 2021, each hauling their own pandemic-frayed marriages and parenting into it. Perceptive about how time reshapes a friendship.

195888551.text: Essays about female friendship, each one anchored in a real friend of Dancyger's, including the cousin she adored who was murdered at twenty. Grief-streaked and unflinching about how much these loves shape us.

198123433.text: A law-school grad teaching tennis in a gated beach enclave gets tangled up with both a divorcee and her daughter. A dark, propulsive thriller that skewers the very rich. Already headed for the screen.

198701985.text: A comedian falls apart after a breakup he doesn't understand, until the last act flips your whole read of it. Funny and true about heartbreak.

199124697.text: Sandwich, by Catherine Newman, describes a family’s week-long vacation in Wellfleet and instantly transported me back. It’s funny, moving, and relatable, much like Newman herself (Aliza and I saw her speak in Boston a few weeks ago.) If you just finished All Fours and aren’t ready to stop thinking/reading about menopause, try Sandwich next.

199345782.text: A big, engrossing novel about a stay-at-home mom coming undone, and the older woman whose friendship reshapes her life. Lombardo writes marriage and parenthood and loneliness better than almost anyone.

199531966.text: A mute man with a waist-length beard, hidden away for decades, is finally discovered and taken to a psychiatric hospital, where an art therapist becomes determined to learn his story. Based on a true case, and so tender about kindness.

199698485.text: A girl vanishes from an Adirondacks summer camp, tangled up with a disappearance years earlier. A character-driven page-turner I tore through.

199796715.text: A broke young single mom starts an OnlyFans and ropes in her ex-wrestler dad. So much more heart and wit than that premise suggests.

199797799.text: If Judy Blume raised you too, this is a love letter and a real argument about how she quietly rewrote what kids were allowed to read. Made me want to reread everything.

199897935.text: Set in 2060, where the rich escape a climate-wrecked coast into private wellness pods floating in the Pacific. Three women's lives intersect in this eerie debut about the true price of convenience.

199897944.text: Postwar Netherlands, a rigid woman and the houseguest she can't stand. It slow-burns and then it detonates. So good.

201102398.text: A novelist chasing a big Hollywood payday tries to sell out gracefully. Sharp and very funny about ambition and identity.

201626978.text: A tennis-champ-turned-housewife climbs into her apartment pool one warm November afternoon in 1957 and simply won't get out. A tiny, tense novel about a marriage cracking open in real time.

201750794.text: Grossman takes on Arthur's knights after Arthur is gone. Big, melancholy, and fun.

203200544.text: A young expat couple in Berlin with the perfectly curated life and a creeping sense that none of it means anything. Short and quietly devastating.

203578896.text: The behind-the-scenes story of Disney Channel's tween golden age, Hilary Duff through Zendaya, built on hundreds of new interviews. Pure nostalgia if you grew up on it.

205524927.text: A memoir by a woman who grew up poor and spent seven years nannying for New York's ultra-wealthy to afford the city. Poignant and funny about class, motherhood, and how rigged the ladder really is.

206340426.text: The very first Discworld, with a hapless wizard playing tour guide to the disc's first tourist. Very silly in the best way, if a bit rougher than the later books.

208474799.text: Pratchett's City Watch arrives, a dragon terrorizes Ankh-Morpork, and it's both hilarious and weirdly wise. A great place to start Discworld.

208511270.text: A woman wakes to the same day, November 18th, over and over, and Balle turns that premise into something quietly hypnotic. The first in a series I did not expect to be so hooked on.

208931300.text: Two brothers grieving their father, both a mess about love. Rooney at her most tender — maybe my favorite of hers.

211025449.text: Ruth and Abe, nearly 70 years married, opposites who somehow made it work. A tender ode to the long haul and all the small forgivenesses it takes.

211399784.text: A fiery ice-dancing duo, told partly like a documentary, with real Wuthering Heights energy. Melodramatic in exactly the way I wanted.

212806569.text: Geraldine Brooks on the sudden death of her husband and the grief she finally let herself feel. Quiet and devastating.

213870076.text: A new mother starts having blackouts, premonitions, and visions of a man who died twenty years ago. Part literary mystery, part something stranger — Walker is so good at that eerie in-between space.

213870083.text: Sittenfeld's short stories are every bit as sharp and funny as her novels. She just gets people.

214151301.text: A very pregnant woman is mid-errand when a massive earthquake levels Portland, and she has to get across the city. Tense, and over almost too fast.

214152261.text: Spare, propulsive, and oddly gripping. It follows one Hungarian man from a rough adolescence into wealth and back, and the flat, stripped-down style sneaks up on you.

214269337.text: A woman finds a newborn hare and, against the odds, ends up raising it. Gentle, patient, unexpectedly moving nature writing.

214269394.text: Two music-obsessed college kids in the early 2000s bond over songs, collaborate, and fall into something complicated. Each chapter is named for a track, and there's a real playlist to go with it. So fun.

214312329.text: Sophie Kinsella wrote this after her own brain tumor diagnosis, about a novelist facing the same. Slim and quietly moving.

215362651.text: A love triangle among college friends traced over fifty years, set against a Montana summer house. Oprah picked it, and it earns the sprawl. About unconditional love and the choices you can't take back.

216247518.text: An actress, a young man who may or may not be her son, and two versions of reality that refuse to line up. Slippery and unsettling in the best way, and no surprise it made the Booker shortlist.

216384422.text: Two sisters split off — one to a Silicon Valley startup, one to Toronto and fertility treatments — in a quiet, thoughtful novel about how tech creeps into everything, even trying to have a baby.

216497043.text: Bourdain's longtime assistant on the food world's hypermasculine underbelly, her own addictions and affairs, and clawing her way to sober. Candid, funny, and genuinely devastating.

216684509.text: Belfast, 1941: across four nights of the Blitz, two sisters — one engaged, one secretly in love with a woman — try to keep living. Intimate, tender, and quietly harrowing.

217245582.text: A Singapore-set debut about two sisters, fierce ambition, and a betrayal that blows the family apart. Emotionally huge — I can see why it became a book club favorite.

217245609.text: The NYT critic on having a baby inside the machine of fertility apps, ultrasounds, gender reveals, freebirth influencers and mommy marketers. Funny and unsettling in equal measure.

217245618.text: A baby is born during the great storm of 1987, and the name his mother chooses splits his life into three timelines across 35 years. A gutting debut about how much one choice can carry.

217387701.text: A sprawling, propulsive family saga about three sisters and the curse hanging over them for decades. It landed on the NYT's ten best books of the year, and I get why.

218460289.text: An Australian in London falls for a divorced journalist, and we follow the decade that builds from there, blended family, motherhood, the slow fight to not disappear into everyone else's needs. Painfully true.

218460337.text: A reality-show dystopia where contestants chase luxury and each other in a desert compound. Sharp on how quickly we'll perform for a prize.

218460342.text: Melissa Febos spends a year celibate and figures out who she is on her own. Smart and searching.

218460347.text: An 80-year-old sets off across the country to win back his high school crush, then gets saddled with two orphaned grandkids and a cat who can predict death. Darkly funny and big-hearted at once.

218539300.text: Six university friends, one year, and the birth, marriage, and death waiting somewhere among them. A warm, globe-hopping celebration of friendship from the author of The Versions of Us.

219301719.text: A pregnant girlfriend shows up on the Samuelsons' doorstep and reshapes a family for decades. Huneven does quiet domestic comedy and real grief better than almost anyone.

220114865.text: A nightclub manager takes a pregnant teenage employee under her wing, tangling up with her ex-husband along the way. Sams is a buzzy young British voice and this debut earns it.

220160387.text: A brilliant, unsettling novel about a real Austrian director who came home from Hollywood to make films under Goebbels. Kehlmann turns the compromises of art under fascism into something you can't look away from. Booker-shortlisted.

220160925.text: A beautiful and comforting read. Gave me new insight/appreciation for USPS, Appalachia, and the profundity of nature and service.

220239049.text: A former contestant's behind-the-scenes memoir of America's Next Top Model and how the sausage really got made. Fun and a little damning.

220239083.text: The true story of a couple whose boat sinks in the Pacific and who survive months adrift on a raft. A gripping, intimate portrait of a marriage under impossible pressure.

221188099.text: Three Belfast women in their thirties, living for the weekend and quietly falling apart a year after losing the fourth in their group. Funny and gutting about friendship, drift, and grief that won't move in a straight line.

222658339.text: Five Black women followed across twenty years of friendship, careers, marriage, motherhood, all the messy middle of adulthood. Flournoy's first since The Turner House and worth the wait.

223001257.text: The protagonist of this beautiful novel is a 73-year-old woman processing her life — and regrets — through letters. It’s poignant but not saccharine, specific but universally appealing. I dare you not to cry.

223436601.text: A former Facebook insider's account of what she saw at the top, and it's genuinely damning. Reads fast and made me furious.

224003127.text: A sliding-doors novel about two happily-married-just-not-to-each-other parents and the affair that plays out in one timeline and stays imagined in the other. Witheringly sharp about millennial marriage.

224076369.text: Two mismatched guys — one brilliant and restless, one a charming mess — build a green-energy startup together across the chaos of the 21st century. Really an ode to male friendship, and better than that makes it sound.

227967141.text: Rocky's back, and this one's even funnier than Sandwich — but also more tender, as a sudden death and a mystery rash send her spiraling into every what-if. Newman never lets me down.

228110489.text: A college love triangle from the '80s reignites decades later when crisis pulls the three back together. Turns out it's Casey from Writers & Lovers all grown up, and King just keeps getting better.

231108670.text: Belle and her seemingly perfect family flee COVID to their gorgeous Martha’s Vineyard home. Abruptly, her husband of two decades tells her he’s no longer in love and leaves. I first mentioned this book in January, and since then, multiple friends have told me they finished it in one session.

231127175.text: The dysfunctional-family debut everyone was texting about this year — savage, funny, and wildly original. Exactly my kind of chaos.

234943545.text: A high school English teacher takes a joke ancestry test from her book club and gets a result that upends her whole family story. Classic Quindlen — warm, wise, all about friendship.

235672456.text: Two couples living across the street from each other divorce and remarry each other basically overnight in 1977 — and this follows the fallout for their kids over decades. From the author of The Nest.

235991949.text: Three strangers — an anxious New Yorker, a newly-sober former TV actor, a burned-out grad student — thrown together on a kitschy reunion cruise days after 9/11. Wry, tender, and quietly devastating about grief and belonging.

235992501.text: From the Blue Ticket author: a heady affair set in a city built to keep desire alive, circling the question of whether anything can really survive 'forever.' Dreamy and a little unsettling.

235992675.text: Six college friends, five parties, twenty years. Ginder does the whole messy arc of friendship — the clinging, the running, the losses — as part love story and part tragicomedy.

235992685.text: A stalled TV writer snoops in her therapist husband's patient notes and just... can't help herself. A laugh-out-loud debut about ambition, envy, and faking it in Hollywood.

238226942.text: A tradwife influencer goes to bed in the present and wakes up actually stranded in the 19th century. Sharp satire and slow-burn suspense at once — no wonder Anne Hathaway snapped up the film rights.

238226950.text: Ten stories with premises that shouldn't work — a woman killed by a crocodile on her honeymoon picks out her appearance for the afterlife; a factory worker falls for an AI sex doll — and absolutely do. I've been a Khong fan since Goodbye, Vitamin, and this collection is her at her strangest and most playful.

238766796.text: A woman reckons with an affair she had with a professor back during the Clinton-Lewinsky years, when he suddenly resurfaces in her life. Funny and pointed about power, men, and who we decide to blame.

239744702.text: An actress and a director orbit each other for fifteen years in Dublin — collaborating, falling out, falling back in. A smart novel about art, muses, and who really owns the work.

240114287.text: A woman turns the tables on her stalker ex by stalking him right back. Profane and funny, with a real reckoning underneath about what surviving abuse actually costs you.

240687665.text: A broke single mom fake-dates a wealthy heir to save her family's seaside house — and, naturally, starts falling for real. Sweet, funny, and exactly the summer comfort read it promises.

240688584.text: 1980s East Village: a woman who can see her friends' ghosts is haunted by the one she can't reach, as AIDS tears through her world. Big-hearted and heartbreaking.

241392662.text: A 35-year-old copywriter and a 23-year-old barista collide in a London bar — and it's less a love story than a tender, sharp look at being broke and adrift in your 20s and 30s. Sally Rooney's a fan.

242252957.text: From the Pineapple Street author: a New Yorker parachutes into a tight seaside-town friend group and stirs everything up. A fun, fast beach read with a little more going on underneath.

242518677.text: From the North Woods guy, but set right now: a family of city academics decamps to rural Vermont for a year. A tender, funny portrait of a dad who's sure he's let everyone down.

242693052.text: Ann Patchett is one of my favorite authors for a reason; I couldn't put this down.

242978423.text: A struggling actor finally lands the role of a lifetime — as personal assistant to a ridiculous Hollywood couple. Razor-sharp and very funny about fame and groveling for it.

243039897.text: A young woman convinced a Pulitzer-winning poet might be her father follows his trail to an NYC MFA program. Buntin's debut Marlena got a ton of love, and this one digs into power — in academia, between men and women, parents and kids.

243497082.text: An ad guy tanks the biggest pitch of his life and decides to just... opt out of capitalism entirely, from his suburban Connecticut backyard. Funny and sharp about ambition and privilege.
